name: Learn: Runtime Security with Falco
description: Learn runtime threat detection with Falco step by step — deploy the Falco DaemonSet, find and read its rule files, author a custom rule that catches a shell in a container, trigger and detect the alert, then tune a rule with a macro/exception so known-good activity stays quiet.
objective: CKS › Runtime Security (20%). Goal: deploy Falco as a DaemonSet, locate its rule files, write a custom rule that detects a shell spawned in a container, trigger and observe the detection, and tune a rule with an exception — the behavioral-detection tasks the CKS weights heavily.

questions.title: Deploy Falco as a DaemonSet
questions.teach:
**Falco** is a runtime-security engine: it watches syscalls from every container on a node and raises alerts when activity matches a **rule** (e.g. a shell spawning, a write to `/etc`, an unexpected outbound connection). Because it must see *every* node's syscalls, Falco runs as a **DaemonSet** — one pod per node (a Deployment/ReplicaSet would miss nodes; a DaemonSet guarantees one agent per node, including new nodes).

**Drivers** — how Falco gets syscall events. Pick one:
- **modern-ebpf** (default, recommended): CO-RE eBPF probe, no compilation, but needs a kernel with **BTF** (`/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux`).
- **ebpf** (legacy): classic eBPF probe (`falco-bpf.o`), broader kernel support.
- **kmod**: kernel module (`falco.ko`), loaded on the host; needs kernel headers to build.
- **plugins/userspace**: no kernel driver at all (e.g. the k8saudit or cloudtrail plugins consuming logs instead of syscalls).
Set via `--set driver.kind=modern-ebpf|ebpf|kmod`.

**Install paths:**
- **Helm** (most common): `helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts`, then `helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace --set driver.kind=modern-ebpf`.
- **Raw manifests**: apply a DaemonSet YAML directly (know that the pod needs `privileged`/host access and `hostPID` to see other processes).

**Gotchas:**
- The pods mount host paths and run **privileged** (or with broad capabilities) — that is expected for a syscall agent, not a misconfiguration.
- modern-ebpf **silently fails to go Ready on a non-BTF kernel**; if pods crash-loop, switch `driver.kind` to `ebpf` or `kmod`.
- Namespace: `--create-namespace` only works with `helm install`; if `falco` already exists, drop it.
- Confirm with `kubectl -n falco get ds,pods` and `kubectl -n falco rollout status ds/falco` — a DaemonSet reports `DESIRED/CURRENT/READY` per node, not replica counts.
questions.prompt:
Install Falco as a DaemonSet in a namespace called `falco`, using the modern-ebpf driver.

Target: a DaemonSet exists in namespace `falco` whose pods run the Falco image (`kubectl -n falco get ds` shows it).
questions.hint: `helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts && helm repo update`, then `helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace --set driver.kind=modern-ebpf`. Check `kubectl -n falco get ds`.
questions.solution:
helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts
helm repo update
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco --namespace falco --create-namespace \
  --set driver.kind=modern-ebpf
kubectl -n falco rollout status ds/falco
kubectl -n falco get ds,pods

verification.description: a Falco DaemonSet exists in namespace 'falco'

questions.title: Confirm Falco is running
questions.teach:
An install isn't finished until Falco's pods are actually **Running and Ready** with their driver loaded and rules parsed. On a non-BTF host the modern-eBPF driver won't load and the pods never become Ready — which is exactly why Falco is a *requires-host* topic. **Where Falco's config and rules live:** - `falco.yaml` — main config (which rule files to load via `rules_file:`, outputs, `json_output`, priority threshold). - Rule files loaded in order; later files override earlier: `falco_rules.yaml` (shipped defaults — **don't edit**), `falco_rules.local.yaml` (**your** overrides/custom rules), plus anything in `/etc/falco/rules.d/`. - With the Helm chart these are rendered into the **`falco` ConfigMap** and mounted into the pods; edit the ConfigMap's `falco_rules.local.yaml` key, not the baked-in defaults. **Verifying health — several angles:** - `kubectl -n falco rollout status ds/falco` — waits for all nodes Ready. - `kubectl -n falco get ds` — compare `DESIRED` vs `READY`. - `kubectl -n falco logs ds/falco` — look for `Falco initialized` / `Loading rules` and any rule parse errors. - `kubectl -n falco describe pod

` — probe failures, driver-load errors, image pull issues. **Gotchas:** - A **bad rule YAML** (indentation, unknown field/macro) makes Falco refuse to start or load — check the logs, not just pod status. - Editing the ConfigMap does **not** restart pods automatically; you must `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco` for a reload. - DaemonSet readiness is per-node: if one node lacks BTF, that one pod stays NotReady while others are fine.
questions.prompt:
Confirm the Falco DaemonSet rolled out — one Falco pod scheduled on every node.

Target: the `falco` DaemonSet's `desiredNumberScheduled` > 0 (a pod per node). On a BTF-enabled host the pods also become Ready; on this bench the eBPF driver can't load, so scheduling is what's graded.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n falco get ds falco` — check `DESIRED`/`CURRENT` (one per node). `kubectl -n falco get pods` shows the per-node pods (they only reach Ready on a BTF host).
questions.solution:
kubectl -n falco get ds falco      # DESIRED = node count, one Falco pod per node
kubectl -n falco get pods -o wide # one falco-* pod scheduled on each node

verification.description: Falco DaemonSet rolled out (one pod scheduled per node)

questions.title: Write a custom rule: shell in a container
questions.teach:
**The three list/rule building blocks** in a Falco rules file (`- rule:`, `- macro:`, `- list:`):
- **`rule`** — the alert. Required keys: `rule:` (name), `desc:`, `condition:`, `output:`, `priority:` (EMERGENCY › ALERT › CRITICAL › ERROR › WARNING › NOTICE › INFO › DEBUG). Optional: `tags:`, `enabled:`, `exceptions:`, `source:` (default `syscall`; others `k8s_audit`, plugin sources).
- **`macro`** — a named reusable `condition:` snippet you reference by name.
- **`list`** — a named set of values used with `in (...)`.

**Condition syntax** is a boolean filter over syscall fields. Common fields: `evt.type` (`execve`, `open`, `connect`), `proc.name`, `proc.cmdline`, `proc.pname`, `container.id`, `fd.name`, `user.name`. Falco ships macros you reuse here:
- `spawned_process` — the event is a process exec (`evt.type in (execve, execveat) and evt.dir=<`).
- `container` — happened inside a container (`container.id != host`).
- `shell_procs` — the program is a shell (bash, sh, zsh, …).
So `condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs`.

**Output fields** use `%`-templated fields, e.g. `%user.name`, `%container.id`, `%proc.cmdline`, `%evt.time`. With `json_output: true` these become structured JSON keys.

**Where to put it & how it loads:**
- Add custom rules to **`falco_rules.local.yaml`** (or a file in `rules.d/`) — never edit the shipped `falco_rules.yaml`; upgrades overwrite it.
- **Override vs append**: a later-loaded rule with the **same name** replaces the earlier one; add `append: true` to extend an existing rule's condition/lists instead of replacing. (In newer rules-file versions the explicit directive is `override:` with `append`/`replace`.)
- With Helm: edit the `falco` ConfigMap key `falco_rules.local.yaml` (`kubectl edit configmap falco` or `helm upgrade --set-file`), then `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco` to reload.

**Gotchas:**
- YAML is indentation-sensitive — a misindented `condition:` or bad macro reference fails the whole load; check `kubectl -n falco logs`.
- Rule **order matters** for same-name overrides; and a rule referencing a macro/list defined *below* it is still fine (file is parsed whole).
- Name it exactly `Terminal shell in container` so the grader can find it.
questions.prompt:
Add a custom rule named `Terminal shell in container` to `falco_rules.local.yaml`. Its condition must detect a shell process spawned inside a container (use `spawned_process`, `container`, and `shell_procs`).

Target: the `falco` ConfigMap's `falco_rules.local.yaml` contains a rule named `Terminal shell in container` whose condition references `spawned_process`, `container`, and `shell_procs`.
questions.hint:
Edit the ConfigMap key `falco_rules.local.yaml` to add:
```
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id)"
  priority: WARNING
```
then `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n falco get configmap falco -o yaml > /tmp/falco-cm.yaml
# append the rule under the falco_rules.local.yaml key, then apply. Example rule body:
cat <<'EOF'
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
EOF
# after editing the ConfigMap:
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco

verification.description: rule 'Terminal shell in container' present with correct condition

questions.title: Trigger the rule and detect the alert
questions.teach:
Now prove the rule fires. To generate the event, exec a shell into any running pod — that spawns a shell inside a container, exactly what your rule matches.

```
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh         # the trigger
kubectl -n falco logs ds/falco | grep "shell in container"   # the detection
```

**Where Falco sends alerts (outputs)** — all configured in `falco.yaml`, several can be on at once:
- **stdout** (`stdout_output`) — the default; read via `kubectl -n falco logs ds/falco`.
- **file** (`file_output` → a path on the node).
- **syslog** (`syslog_output`).
- **program/shell** (`program_output`, e.g. pipe to a webhook).
- **gRPC** (`grpc_output`) — consumed by **falcosidekick**, which fans out to Slack, Elasticsearch, Loki, etc.
- `json_output: true` turns every alert into structured JSON (easier to `grep`/parse).
- `priority:` in `falco.yaml` sets the **minimum** severity that is emitted — a rule below the threshold stays silent even when it matches.

**Triggering & confirming (exam):** run a throwaway pod (`kubectl run tmp --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600`), `kubectl exec` a shell into it, then grep the Falco logs for your output text. `kubectl logs ds/falco` shows one pod's logs; to catch the alert you may need the pod on the **same node** as the triggering pod (or check each pod / use `-l`).

**Runtime note (requires a BTF host):** actually *observing* the alert needs a running modern-ebpf probe, which needs a kernel with BTF. On this bench (Docker Desktop LinuxKit, no BTF) the probe can't load, so the alert cannot be produced here and this step is graded on the closest verifiable artifact instead: that the `Terminal shell in container` rule is **enabled** (not disabled/commented out) in the loaded local rules. On a real exam cluster you would see the line appear in `kubectl -n falco logs ds/falco`.

**Gotchas:**
- `enabled: false` on a rule (or commenting it out) silently stops detection even though the DaemonSet is healthy.
- A matching event below the `priority` threshold produces **no** output — raise the threshold or the rule priority.
- Buffering/time: newly added rules only apply after a **rollout restart**; the trigger must happen *after* the reload.
questions.prompt:
Confirm the detection path is live: ensure the `Terminal shell in container` rule is enabled in `falco_rules.local.yaml` (not `enabled: false` and not commented out), so that execing a shell into a pod would produce an alert in Falco's logs.

Target: in the `falco` ConfigMap, the `Terminal shell in container` rule is present and enabled (RUNTIME detection requires a BTF host — graded here on the enabled rule artifact).
questions.hint: If you added `enabled: false` or commented the rule out, re-enable it. A Falco `- rule:` entry is enabled by default; an explicit `enabled: false` under it disables it. Then `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco` and, on a BTF host, `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh` then `kubectl -n falco logs ds/falco | grep 'shell in container'`.
questions.solution:
# Trigger (works on a BTF host):
kubectl run trip --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sleep 3600
kubectl exec -it trip -- sh -c 'echo hi'
# Detect (BTF host):
kubectl -n falco logs ds/falco | grep "shell in container"
# Here (no BTF): make sure the rule is enabled in falco_rules.local.yaml
kubectl -n falco get configmap falco -o jsonpath='{.data.falco_rules\.local\.yaml}'

verification.description: rule 'Terminal shell in container' is enabled (closest artifact; live detect needs BTF host)

questions.title: Tune the rule with an exception
questions.teach:
Real clusters have known-good shell activity (a sidecar, a health-check script) that would flood you with false positives. You **tune** a rule rather than delete it. The common tuning techniques:

1. **`exceptions:`** (preferred, native) — a list on the rule. Each entry has a `name:`, `fields:` (the syscall fields to check), optional `comps:` (per-field operators — defaults to `=`/`in`), and `values:`. A match in any exception makes the rule **not** fire. Multiple `fields` in one exception are ANDed. Example skips when `proc.name` is in an allow-list.
2. **`and not <macro>`** — define `- macro: allowed_shell_procs` (`condition: proc.name in (my-healthcheck)`) and append `and not allowed_shell_procs` to the rule's `condition:`.
3. **`append: true` / `override:`** — extend the *shipped* rule's condition or its lists without copying the whole rule (e.g. add entries to a trusted-images list the default rule already consults).
4. **Disable** (`enabled: false`) — last resort; silences the rule entirely instead of narrowing it.

Exceptions vs macro: an **exception** is scoped to one rule and is the maintainable choice; the `and not macro` edits the condition directly and can be reused across rules.

Add a tuning so a known-good process named `my-healthcheck` does **not** alert.

**Gotchas:**
- `fields`, `comps`, and `values` must line up: with two `fields`, each `values` row is a list of two, and `comps` (if given) lists one operator per field.
- Values that match a `list` form (`in`) are wrapped in brackets: `values: - [my-healthcheck]`.
- Don't delete or wholesale-rewrite the default rule to tune it — use `exceptions`/`append` so upgrades still work.
- Reload after editing: `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.
- Name the exception `known_good` (or define a macro referenced as `allowed_shell_procs`) so the grader can find your tuning.
questions.prompt:
Tune `Terminal shell in container` so a process named `my-healthcheck` does not fire the rule. Add an `exceptions:` entry named `known_good` on the rule (listing `proc.name`), or add a macro and `and not ...` it into the condition.

Target: the `falco` ConfigMap's `falco_rules.local.yaml` contains either an exception named `known_good` or a tuning macro, referencing `my-healthcheck`.
questions.hint:
Under the rule add:
```
  exceptions:
  - name: known_good
    fields: [proc.name]
    comps: [in]
    values:
    - [my-healthcheck]
```
or define `- macro: allowed_shell_procs` with `condition: proc.name in (my-healthcheck)` and append `and not allowed_shell_procs` to the rule condition. Then `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.
questions.solution:
# Append exceptions to the rule in falco_rules.local.yaml:
cat <<'EOF'
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id)"
  priority: WARNING
  exceptions:
  - name: known_good
    fields: [proc.name]
    comps: [in]
    values:
    - [my-healthcheck]
EOF
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco

verification.description: exception/macro for 'my-healthcheck' present in local rules
